Update: Bubble boy

By: Ofentse Lamola | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
He was born without an immune system and given almost no chance of survival. Today he’s thriving, but what about the children who come after him?

Unique Selling Point:
A rare long-term follow-up on a South African first. Nearly a decade after receiving groundbreaking gene therapy for Severe Combined Immunodeficiency, Ayaan Ahmed Sheik is thriving. His story offers a powerful human outcome to a once-experimental treatment. But while the science has progressed globally, access in South Africa remains limited. This update combines an emotional revisit with a critical look at whether meaningful change has followed.

Summary:
When Carte Blanche first told the story of Ayaan Ahmed Sheik in 2018, he was a critically ill toddler born without an immune system, living in strict isolation and battling life-threatening infections.

At the time, his only chance of survival was an experimental gene therapy trial at St Jude Children’s Research Hospital in the United States. After a long and uncertain journey, the treatment was declared a success, and Ayaan returned home to South Africa.

Now, eight years later, Ayaan is living a full and active life. He is in primary school, no longer dependent on chronic medication or a feeding tube, and has developed a natural talent for music, playing the piano by ear. His progress offers rare insight into the long-term success of gene therapy for SCID.

But this update is not only about survival. While Ayaan’s outcome represents a medical breakthrough, access to similar treatment remains extremely limited for South African patients. Gene therapy is now becoming more widely available internationally, yet it is still not accessible locally.

At the same time, the issue of newborn screening, first raised in the original story, remains largely unresolved. A simple test at birth could have identified Ayaan’s condition early and prevented years of trauma and medical intervention.

This update revisits Ayaan’s journey through the eyes of his mother, Shamaa, while asking a broader question: if a child were born with SCID in South Africa today, would their outcome be any different?

Further information:
1. SEVERE COMBINED IMMUNODEFICIENCY (SCID)
SCID is one of the most severe primary immunodeficiencies, leaving children without a functioning immune system. Incidence is estimated at roughly 1 in 50,000 births globally. Without early diagnosis and treatment, most children do not survive beyond early childhood.

In South Africa, the condition is likely underdiagnosed due to the lack of a universal newborn screening programme.

2. GENE THERAPY: GLOBAL PROGRESS VS LOCAL ACCESS
At the time of Ayaan’s treatment, gene therapy was still in the clinical trial phase. Since then, advances in lentiviral gene therapy have improved both safety and long-term outcomes. Treatment is now being offered in specialised centres internationally.

However, access remains highly restricted. In South Africa, gene therapy for SCID is not part of standard care and is not locally available, meaning families would still need to seek treatment abroad.

3. AYAAN’S LONG-TERM OUTCOME
Nearly a decade after his treatment, Ayaan’s progress demonstrates the long-term success of gene therapy. He is healthy, active, and no longer dependent on medical interventions that once defined his life.

Key milestones include:

Full removal of feeding tube dependency
No need for chronic medication
Normal schooling and development
Emerging talent in music, particularly piano

His case provides rare longitudinal insight into the durability of gene therapy outcomes.

4. NEWBORN SCREENING
Newborn screening remains a central issue. A simple heel-prick test at birth can detect SCID early, allowing for immediate intervention and significantly improved outcomes.

In South Africa, screening is still not routinely implemented and is largely limited to private healthcare settings. Awareness remains low, despite its potential to prevent severe illness and reduce long-term healthcare costs.

5. ADVOCACY AND AWARENESS
Since Ayaan’s recovery, his mother Shamaa has become an advocate for immune deficiency awareness.

The update aligns with World Primary Immunodeficiency Week, creating a strong editorial link between Ayaan’s personal journey and broader awareness efforts.

The story also ties into Freedom Day, marking the anniversary of Ayaan’s “freedom from the bubble”, adding emotional and symbolic weight to the update.

Script:


(Voiceover) Little Ayaan was only a year old when St. Jude Children’s Research Hospital in the US offered him a chance at a normal childhood.

(Shamaa Sheik) To save my one child, I had to leave the country and leave another child behind.

(Voiceover) Shamaa Sheik took her son to Memphis, Tennessee, for specialised gene therapy developed under the leadership of Dr Ewelina Mamcarz (pr. Mamshars).

(Dr Ewelina Mamcarz, Carte Blanche 2018) Briefly, Gene therapy restores a normal copy of the defective gene. We collect this bone marrow in a procedure called harvest and then infect the cells with a virus, disabled HIV virus. It carries the normal copy of the gene into the stem cells.

(Voiceover) By the time the treatment ended, Ayaan had spent most of his life in isolation – a sanitised world, with little human interaction.

(Shamaa Sheik) He reached a world that he couldn’t touch. He touched a world that he couldn’t be a part of. And that was, for me, the most depressing part about this entire journey.

(Voiceover) Back home, he had an extended family, eager to meet him.

(Shamaa Sheik) So, he was cleared to finally have human contact. And so I decided to surprise my parents by taking him on his first trip to visit my broader family in Durban. And I think that for me was one of the most memorable moments that we achieved.

(Voiceover) But the journey was far from over.

(Shamaa Sheik) His physician in Memphis at the time said to me, “You know, he will be on a feeding tube for the rest of his life.” And I thought that’s a tough thing to be able to accept.

(Voiceover) But he surprised everyone, and today, you’d never know that Ayaan once had no chance of a normal life, and little chance of surviving his childhood.

(Shamaa Sheik) He’s healthy, he’s happy. He’s eating and drinking by mouth with no issues at all.

(Ayaan Sheik, home video) I’m so lucky to be born from an Indian girl.
(Shamaa Sheik) Why?
(Ayaan Sheik) Because you make very nice food, hey.

(Voiceover) He’s now in Grade Three and no longer needs chronic medication. And he’s exploring everything life has to offer.

(Shamaa Sheik) He plays by ear. He’s been playing by ear since he was seven.

(Voiceover) The St Jude medical team continues to monitor Ayaan's progress. And the treatment that saved his life is now commercially available.

(Dr Ali Suliman) Overall, it is more available now. It's still in clinical trial in more centres in Europe and in the US. Unfortunately, back in Africa and South Africa, the mainstay of the standard of care is still bone marrow transplant. We are working to make it more accessible to more kids like Ayaan, but it is good to see that in the future.

(Voiceover) As our country observes Freedom Day tomorrow, Ayaan and his family will celebrate a more personal milestone: the eighth anniversary of Ayaan’s freedom from the bubble.

(Shamaa Sheik) In hindsight I think what an incredible journey. I don’t think I would ever have imagined coming out of this the way that we have, with a child so healthy, a child who’s thriving, a child who should not have been alive. And you are just filled with this immense sense of gratitude.

ADVOCACY AND AWARENESS Since Ayaan’s recovery, his mother Shamaa has become an advocate for immune deficiency awareness. The update aligns with World Primary Immunodeficiency Week, creating a strong editorial link between Ayaan’s personal journey and broader awareness efforts. The story also ties into Freedom Day, marking the anniversary of Ayaan’s “freedom from the bubble”, adding emotional and symbolic weight to the update.
